structure.title: Meditations I–II · A house of beliefs is emptied
structure.text: Dreams and a possible deceiver let Descartes withdraw assent from more and more things. The act of being deceived leaves one activity in place, and the changing piece of wax tests what the remaining thinker can actually claim to know.

structure.title: Meditations III–V · Rebuild trust in judgment
structure.text: Descartes inventories his ideas, argues for a non-deceiving God and asks how error is possible for a creature of such a maker. The relation between what one understands and what one is willing to affirm becomes decisive.

structure.title: Meditation VI · Return to a body that feels
structure.text: Hunger, pain and a misleading thirst complicate the recovery of the material world. A thinker can distinguish mind from body in argument and still experience an injury as something happening intimately to them.

people.name: The meditator
people.role: A first-person role the reader can occupy
people.text: The order of discoveries matters. An assurance available on the sixth day cannot simply be borrowed on the first, when even the reliability of a simple calculation is under deliberate suspicion.

people.name: The deceiver
people.text: The thought experiment asks what would remain certain under the worst imaginable epistemic conditions. It needs the possibility of deception to do its work, which is a much smaller commitment than belief in such a being.

context.title: The six days form an exercise
context.text: Familiar beliefs return as soon as attention wanders. Descartes describes that pull as part of the inquiry, since knowing the words of a sceptical argument and sustaining its effect on one's own judgment are different achievements.

notice.text: Follow the wax toward the fire.
notice.why: Colour, smell, sound and firmness alter, yet we judge that the wax remains. The ordinary confidence of that judgment is the very thing Descartes asks an account of perception to explain.

notice.text: Notice the difference between feeling pain and locating it.
notice.why: A sensation can be unmistakable as an experience and still mislead its owner about where the trouble lies. This helps explain why restoring trust in the senses leaves room for bodily error.

opening: Descartes sits down to discard every belief that could be false. His senses have deceived him; dreams have felt real; perhaps even his reasoning is being manipulated. Once the demolition begins, ordinary assurances offer little help. These six meditations follow an attempt to find something that survives doubt and then rebuild a world from it. The excitement lies in how much has to be risked for certainty, and how carefully each apparently secure step needs inspecting before the next can bear weight.
